utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I was informed that you wanted to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are quite right, Mr. President. I shall be as brief as possible. I thank you for giving me the floor, Mr. President. The reason why, that is, the Defence wanted to address the Chamber very briefly concerns both the testimony of the witness that we are going to hear shortly and another matter. As for this other matter is concerned, when the French General was examined yesterday, the Prosecution wanted to help the Defence in order to help the Defence with the references of the text, which made us lose a lot of time because the references were not correct. I am talking about the page and the paragraph. So if we are going to save the time, I don't think that that is the right procedure. So we would like that, in future, the intervention of the Prosecution should be made in a different language, not English, and as efficiently as possible. And we would also wish that these interventions be accurate, which yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we are not going to discuss what happened yesterday. It is in my mind that the Prosecution tried to assist you and that by -- caused by some unlucky circumstances, small mistakes, that their intention did not work out as they wished it would. Let's not spend time. Mistakes will be there. I am not going to say that there is more mistakes here or there. Let's not spend too much time on that. Please come to your next matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second matter which is a more important one is the following: It regards the witness Richard Mole, the one that we are going to hear shortly. As far as this witness is concerned, the Defence, as they indicated yesterday, is not going to continue its cross-examination except under certain reservations. Specifically, the Defence notes that there has been a contact between the Prosecution and the witness. Although we asked the witness to leave the courtroom, that is, we asked that the witness be asked to leave the courtroom, the Prosecution clearly stated their position. They even indicated that, as far as they were concerned, they consider Lukavica, that is General Galic, to be responsible for -- no, Mr. President, I really wish to continue because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, am I correct when a similar complaint was made yesterday and that we gave ruling on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wish to ask the Chamber to reconsider its decision. When the Defence is asking the Chamber to reconsider its decision, the Defence is very often interrupted, whereas this is not the case with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your request is that we reconsider the decision. I will then now allow you to add to what has been said yesterday, whatever is new in respect of that. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of what has been yesterday. Until now -- I should check precisely, but 95 to 98 per cent sounded rather familiar in my ears. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what is new, but I say that I cannot express it the way I would like to express it, we are now addressing a specific request. We wish that this witness simply be excluded from the witness list because -- and this is a new element -- because all of the cross-examination that we can conduct will necessarily have as its result of the examination of the witness something which is not regular in terms of procedure. And that is the reason why we are addressing this formal request to the Chamber to strike the witness from the list of witnesses and to fulfill our application. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will consult first within the Chamber, after I have given the opportunity to Mr. Ierace to respond very briefly, only to those aspects that are new, and that is that the witness should be stricken from the list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have nothing to add to the submissions that I made yesterday. I think they apply just as well to this fresh course of action that my friend seeks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should add that, if you wish, I would take you to those submissions yesterday, if it is required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have the submissions on my computer. Well, it is around page 11.005, that is where I find them. And I am just checking more in detail what you exactly told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If it saves time, I can recap them in two sentences. The first is that nothing I said went outside the evidence the witness had already given and, therefore, there can be no contamination of the witness's evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber prefers to withdraw for a moment because it's not the most easy way to deliberate, looking to the left and to the right. We need a bit more time. If everyone would please stand by. And could I have a written transcript of yesterday. I have it on my computer now, but I can't take the computer with me. --- Break taken at 9.17 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has taken the effort to re-read again the transcript of yesterday and notices that it was the witness, Mr. Mole, himself who mentioned already the Croatian aspects, the Croatian attacks, as I may call them so in respect of Lukavica. If there would have been any contamination, and it is a rather complex matter seeing the evidence he gave already, the part of the reports, but if there would be any contamination in respect of these Croatian attacks and the role of Lukavica and/or the accused, then this contamination would have been adequately dealt with by sustaining the objection and not admitting any further questions on the aspects which are, I would say, outside Sarajevo. The Chamber finds, as it did yesterday, no reason to exclude, in general terms, the evidence of this witness, apart from the exclusion of further questions yesterday. This Chamber consists of professional Judges and we will carefully take into account when evaluating evidence or assessing the probative value of evidence the concerns of the Defence in respect of the -- of what they consider to be contamination. That is the ruling. So the Defence may continue the cross-examination they started already yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to thank the Chamber. For the record, simply, note should be taken that we will probably appeal the decision pursuant to Article 73(B). So the cross-examination will continue but under the same reservations that I have already indicated. Omission in the French booth: And/or the accused in line 5.23 and/or I am just taking the opportunity when the witness is not present in the courtroom to draw attention to this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, page 5, line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, good morning. I am sorry that you had to wait for more time than perhaps you would have expected. Ms. Pilipovic, you may proceed after I remind you, Mr. Mole, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mole.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I continue with my cross-examination, Mr. Mole, I should like you to explain to us in a little more detail the answer that you gave yesterday in response to a question asked by my learned colleague. It actually happened on several occasions. Your answer was: "I believe that this was the case, that this is so." Am I correct in having understood your answers on several occasions as having been, "Yes, I think that this is so."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: We are not quoting witness's words because we do not have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question doesn't seem to make a lot of sense. My learned colleague has given the answers but hasn't given the questions, or perhaps she could give some sense of the question, some clue as to the context of the answer: "I believe that this was the case, that this is so."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, we've got on our screen a message from the interpreters that they are not quoting witness's words because the interpreters have no transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not quoting witness's responses. I merely wanted the witness to confirm to us that that was more or less what he said. It was just my interpretation of his words. Page 43 of yesterday's transcript, for example, witness's answer was, and I should like to hear the confirmation of the witness: "I believe that this is so." Perhaps I am not quoting it accurately; I am paraphrasing his words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, Ms. Pilipovic would like to know that if you use words such as "I believe that it was the case," whether you then mean to say, "Yes, I think that it is so."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I given an affirmative, "yes," then I was there at the time and I am positive of my answer. If I wasn't present at the event that is being discussed but I believe that that was the case, that's when I would use that expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the problem with my learned colleague not contextualising the answer with the question because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is clear now, I think, that a general answer could not be given in this respect. That's what you tell us: "It depends on when I use these words that I've not been present and I gave the answer on the basis of the information I had which could be -- " well, whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I might say, I did qualify my answers by suggesting that I wasn't, for example, at the meeting in June 1992 and, therefore, any answer I gave about that meeting would be, "I believe so" because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Mr. Mole. Just to clarify, when you say you were not there but believed that that was the case, are you confirming that you -- are you telling us that you are not sure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that it is about June 1992, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't ask the witness about any specific example, but the witness himself provided us with an example. If he said that that was in the month of June and he was not there, he told us that he was not sure. I am asking in general in cases when he was not there. But when he said that he believed that that was the case, I wanted him to confirm that he is actually not sure that that was the case if he was not present then and there or if he did not attend a meeting or a conversation during his tour of duty, that is, from September until December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, please ask the witness, but he made clear that he chooses his words according to the circumstances of what he is asked about. So whether it is of any use to ask this in general terms... But please proceed and we will hear what the answer will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us summarise this question and your answer in a sense that what you are saying is that where you were, where you were present, when you say, "I believe so," then you are certain that this is so? Did I understand your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I try to repeat your answer and see whether my understanding as well and whether Ms. Pilipovic would then agree. Did you explain to us that when you use the words "I believe so," that you have to make this reservation because you were not present at the event you were asked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am prepared to qualify in contextual terms all my answers from now on, if that will assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, well, that is more or less what we -- please ask in contextual terms an explanation of the answer of the witness and not in general terms any more. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, you told us yesterday that you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in September 1997 and at one point, when there was a question raised regarding Mr. Kosovac, you told us then - and I am going to interpret your words - you said that what you said was a statement given five years ago and that, at this point, you could not now interpret the events the way you interpreted them five years ago. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. What I said was, I could not recall, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sitting here, the function of the individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you confirm to us that your statement regarding the events in the relevant period of time in Sarajevo, while you were in Sarajevo, and what you told the investigators in 1997, could you confirm that your memory then was a lot fresher than it is now and that you were able to be more accurate when you gave your statement then regarding those events in question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mole. Yesterday, we spoke of the Airport Agreement from June 1992, and you confirmed to us that this was an important step that was undertaken in order to separate the warring factions in the city. Did you personally have an opinion about this agreement and about this measure that was taken on both sides? So what was your assessment of this measure taken by both sides? Specifically, what I mean is: What did you think about it from the point of view from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task in Sarajevo was not to regard any action or agreement from one side as opposed to the other. My task was to interpret the Airport Agreement and invoke its terms. My opinion about the agreement was irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, I will remind you, you said in your statement on page 0090149, you said that, regarding the Serb side, this step in handing over the airport from the very beginning of the conflict should be appreciated considering that the Serbs were in a position of -- tactically, in a battle position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this position that you just confirmed, was this also appreciated in the same way in other circles of military observers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a military assessment and so clearly the military observers would appreciate it as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, at that time when you were on duty, was there a balance of sorts between the warring factions that you could personally make an assessment of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may divide my answer into two parts: Firstly, militarily, there was significant difference between the two sides in terms of disposition, quantity, quality, of forces. There was a status quo as relates to the front line which remained virtually intact throughout my tour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, within the Airport Agreement, could you confirm to us -- and I think that this was one of your tasks, to make sure that the ceasefire is implemented between the warring parties. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a function of UN military observers to maintain the terms of a ceasefire, should that condition prevail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say that you were making sure that these conditions are respected, could you tell us how much did you know, to what extent did the warring parties respect this ceasefire? And I am talking about the period while you were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my tenure in Sarajevo, there was only one ceasefire signed on the 11th of November, 1992, remembering that the June agreement was before I appeared in Sarajevo. That was meant to be a city-wide ceasefire. Of course, we performed our functions to monitor that ceasefire and insist upon it but, in reality, the level of violence only reduced after that ceasefire. So there was never really an effective ceasefire throughout my tenure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, you just told us that the first ceasefire came into force in June 1992. Did you, from your predecessor that you took over from as the commander, did you have any information from him that during the period between August, July, there were any breaches or violations of this ceasefire agreement by the BH army which at the time was in the process of carrying out operation called Jug? [Realtime transcript read in error "Uke"] Did you have any such information, did you receive it? And that this operation was an offensive operation which lasted until September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the transcript, I can see that translation, I believe that the name of the operation is "Jug", that is J-u-g; that means "south."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for your assistance. Would you answer the question, Mr. Mole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just read the question again on the screen, please. My predecessor did not explain to me that there had been any particular operation on either side during the period prior to my arrival in Sarajevo. But what was clear was that there had been no ceasefire during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of this period and the ceasefire that was agreed on the 11th of November, 1992. Since you were there at the time, could you perhaps tell us whether in that period there were violations of the ceasefire, specifically by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The level of violence reduced after the 11th of November for a period of approximately seven days. But at no stage in that period or any other whilst I was in Sarajevo was there an effective ceasefire on either side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please answer: Which side was violating the ceasefire? Specifically, I will remind you that for the 18th of November, 1992, in the monthly report, it was written that the Presidency had carried out an attack in the area of Zuc.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have the monthly report. I have the date of the 18th of November, 1992, but the question asked by my friend really now is in two parts. The first part of that is simply which side was violating the ceasefire; and the second part is, in effect, a drawing of the witness's attention in a way which detracts from the ability to fairly answer the first question, the first part of the question. So I would ask that it be split into two, the witness answer the first part and then comment on the second part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, yes, could you please do so because I noticed before that sometimes you put five questions in one and that might confuse the witness. So, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, could you tell us, in the period from the -- from when the ceasefire agreement was signed in November, as you told us, in 1992 - I believe that was the 11th of November - according to what you can recall, who -- which side violated, broke, the agreement, the ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstand the circumstances that the ceasefire was signed within. I have, I think, clearly indicated that all that occurred after the ceasefire being signed was a reduction in the level of violence, which lasted a week. So, therefore, to ask me which side violated the ceasefire is not a question which can be answered because there was no effective ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mole. According to what you can recall, can you tell us whether in November 1992 there was a plan on the side of the BH army offensive operation called "Koverat" or "envelope"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us in which areas of the city were operations taken, or rather, where offensive operations taken by the BH army in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I clarify the role of the Senior Military Observer in Sarajevo in answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, I just wanted you to answer about what you knew in relation to the operation Koverat, their extent and whether you have any knowledge, any information. If you don't, you can just say so.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in the course of your stay, your mandate, in Sarajevo from your military observers who covered the observation posts of Lima and Papa, did you receive any information about offensive operations of the BH army in the period of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any information of a military nature that we received from either side was very carefully controlled, obviously, by each side. So the only information which we were able to receive and assess was that given to us from the other side and their perceptions of military threat. That is, therefore, not a good basis upon which to take action or for me to answer your question definitively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, did you, from your military observers who were at their posts in the month of November, did you receive information that the forces, as it was usually reported in monthly reports, that the forces of the Presidency were launching attacks in the area of Zuc in November? Could you confirm that such reports were received and whether they were correct? Did you check them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive such reports and, yes, they were correct and, yes, I visited Zuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, when you say that you visited Zuc, could you tell us which observation post was located in the area of Zuc and what was the concentration of weapons and troops of the BH army in that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no observation point at Zuc. That was the reason I visited Zuc. I was hosted by the Serb side. And the disposition of the Presidency forces was difficult to assess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when or whether there was ever an observation post located in the area of Zuc, a Papa point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I visited in Zuc there was no Papa location that looked over the whole area, for it was a very large, mountainous region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, could you tell us whether in the period while you were the commander in Sarajevo, whether in the area of Zuc there were battles fought between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. And might I remind you that the map which we saw earlier in my evidence, if I remember correctly, had a dotted line in the area of Zuc and that, in military map marking circles, is accepted as an area where the front line is constantly changing, which confirms my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you confirm that there were battles fought, could you perhaps specify at what time in December, when were these battles fought, and could you describe perhaps the intensity of the battles?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I remind you that we had no constant observation point overlooking Zuc. We were aware that it was a significant area for conflict, but because we were unable to monitor it and view it ourselves, it was very difficult for us to quantify the actions in that area. So I cannot give any further detail other than I have given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you say that you cannot give any further detail, could you perhaps answer whether the consequences of the battles that were fought in that period in the area of Zuc, and bearing in mind the monthly reports the Defence has that was in December, the consequences of these battles, could they be felt in the populated area, were in the populated area of that location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection of the area in question is that it was lightly populated. Are you referring to those lightly populated areas on Zuc?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was thinking in general terms of the populated areas in the vicinity of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Where the area was populated, there would have been significant effect of the events that you are discussing, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what was the closest observation post from the Papa positions that could have observed the area of Zuc in the month of December? Was that the observation post next to the PTT building, Papa 5, or another observation post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right in that Papa 5 was the nearest to Zuc, but it overlooked the city and was only partway up the high ground and, therefore, had no vision towards or over Zuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are confirming to us that from the location of Papa 5, it was not possible to follow any activities in the area of Zuc?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, except for obviously hearing any rounds that were being fired or were landing. But that is not an accurate observation of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I see that we are both looking at the clock at the same time. We will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would first like to inform the parties that they can expect a written decision either today or tomorrow in respect of the expert witnesses, Philips and Tabeau, and the decision will be that Mr. Philips and Mr. Tabeau can be examined and cross-examined as expert witnesses. So the objection from the Defence is denied in that respect. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, two matters very quickly, and I think that both can be dealt with in the presence of the witness. Yesterday, I indicated that I would be tendering some documents in relation to this witness where I would be relying on the contents of the documents, whether portions have specifically been brought to the attention of the witness or not. For the assistance of my friends during cross-examination, I should specify that, in that regard, I propose to tender in their entirety the three monthly reports, that is, October, November, December. Secondly, Mr. President, at some stage might I respectfully suggest that we allow a little time to discuss a broader timetable issue, specifically, the post end-of-Prosecution timetable, the amount of time for submissions and the pre-Defence trial conference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will certainly find time to discuss this on a rather short notice. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As regards two expert witnesses that you have mentioned, the Defence will examine, if necessary, these witnesses under the same caveat, the save reservations, because we have already indicated that we intend to appeal the decision. As for the matters brought up by Mr. Ierace, I understood that one Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the reports was withdrawn yesterday and that it was not even submitted to the witness. I don't know whether we are talking about the same report or not, but at any rate, I think that that one has been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... where we have to decide upon it and then Mr. Ierace can explain. It is not always necessarily done in the presence of the witness. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, before the break we discussed Papa 5 observation post. Can you confirm for us that it was located in the vicinity of the PTT building, where the UN military observers were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the one observation point nearest to the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tenure, from your observation post, Papa 5, that is, did you receive reports on the activity of the mortar belonging to the Presidency which was located in the vicinity of the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall a permanent location of a mortar near the PTT building because we would not have permitted that, in that it would naturally draw fire to the PTT building. But I was aware of the mobility of the Presidency side using mortars from the backs of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the calibre of these movable mortars? Did you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we had no information regarding that because you will recall that one of the functions of the UN military observers was to invoke the Airport Agreement, which included weapon collection areas, but we were quite aware that there were weapons on both sides which had not been collected and were, therefore, not monitored.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us, Mr. Mole, that there were weapons on both sides which you and your staff were unable to control?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I clarify? We would never be able to control weapons. The term I have used is "monitor." With that regard, yes, there were weapons on both sides but we were unable to monitor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, Mr. Mole, were there any other locations in the area of Papa observation posts from where you received reports on the activity of mortars, mobile mortars?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. I recall particularly a series of incidents which involved such weapons around the area of the Kosevo hospital in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we spoke about the activity of BH army mobile mortars in the area of the PTT building and the Kosevo hospital, can you tell us, to the best of your recollection, how frequent such incidents were? During your tenure, of course.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can say that it was a frequent occurrence. It was extremely hard to monitor, but in an attempt to do so, I introduced mobile patrolling, especially on the Papa side, in an attempt to suppress or at least monitor the events we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you tasked your observers with establishing the location of the incident involving mobile mortars. Did you receive any information as to the area where these mobile mortars were active? I am referring to the area covered by Papa observation post.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were, however, in the unfortunate position of being reactive to these incidents and were clearly not able to pre-empt them because we were not in a position to have prior information of their use in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, during your tenure in Sector Sarajevo, was Mr. Bezrouchenko Chief of UNPROFOR, Chief of Staff in this area? Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the name but since you mentioned Chief of Staff in UNPROFOR sector headquarters, I dealt directly with a Colonel Davout of the French military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your mandate, did you at any point in time receive information to the effect that there was an ammunition factory in the basement of the PTT building, which ammunition was intended for the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that that was the case, but it was unfounded information in that, being the Senior Military Observer, I had to be sure in my mind that the PTT building was not being used for such inappropriate activity. I confirmed that that had not been the case. There was an engineering workshop but it was not producing any munitions, not during my tour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mole. You were, as a commander, chief of UNMOs in the area. One of your tasks was to repair the infrastructure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how frequent such missions were during your tenure and what exactly was the cause of damage to the infrastructure? I am referring, obviously, to the area of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My predecessor did not involve himself on what may I call, "utility missions." It was me that invoked them. We would plan one or two a week. I created a team specifically to fulfill this role and preceded every operation with an intense amount of preparation: informing both sides of the intentions of the teams, assembling the workers necessary and providing them the protection they required. In answer to your question of the damage of the infrastructure, it was extremely significant and our intentions were to restore some power and some water to those sections of the city that the utility missions addressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Mole, that the -- this damage to the infrastructure as far as the power and water are concerned was caused in the area of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Much of the damage was effected on the front lines, which made the nature of the missions extremely dangerous, and hence my reference to the detail planning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, in your statement, the one that you gave in 1997, when asked questions about the role and the purpose of your mission, you stated - I paraphrase - that over 50 per cent -- in over 50 per cent of the cases, fire was opened from both sides. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was expected that most utility missions would be subjected to fire from one side or the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the consequences of this damage are concerned, what was their effect on various neighbourhoods in the town of Sarajevo in terms of shortages of electricity and water, and in what period of time was this emphasised?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout my tenure in Sarajevo, the loss of running clean water was probably the most significant of the shortages. Electricity was seldom available, and if it was available, it would be for a very short period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of the observation posts, Papa and Lima observation posts, in the area of Nedzarici, was there any such observation post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I inherited an observation post in Nedzarici which had been set up by my predecessor very shortly before I arrived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that that particular observation post was located at the front line and that it was the Serbs who had requested the setting up of this observation post in the area of Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Nedzarici was an enclave into the city, an extremely difficult area for the commander, and we well understood his desire to have an UN presence with him. However, as its intention was to observe the city, this could not be achieved from the selected location. So with limited manpower, I redeployed the individuals elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, it is true, is it not, that the area in question, Nedzarici, was one of the most sensitive locations in the town and that the Presidency forces exerted constant -- strong and constant pressure over this area in terms of military attacks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I completely agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about the commander, did you also speak about the commander of the military formation which belonged to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps which was deployed in the area, the commander that had requested the presence of the UN as a form of protection?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I assume you mean the local commander in Nedzarici, and if that is what you are saying, I understand he requested the presence of the UN, but remember that was before I arrived in Sarajevo. But I did discuss with him the usefulness of the UN observation post in his location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you withdrew this observation post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you spent some time in the area of Nedzarici and in view of the fact that this was a very sensitive portion of the front line, can you tell us how far the two front lines were apart in this area? How far apart were the two sides in this area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Literally, a few metres in some places, a hundred metres in another. Very close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you confirm for us that this was an area which was constantly under heavy fighting, was exposed to heavy fighting, daily heavy fighting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, according to what you can recollect, could you please tell us where were the positions of the BH army in the area of Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you recall, I had marked the front line on the map which has already been submitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mole. I have before me this map, but my question was whether you could tell us where the BH army was located or, rather, accommodated in the area of the front line near Nedzarici or, rather, the disposition of the forces, where were they, in which buildings there; how many were there? If you could perhaps tell us a little more about that area.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the specific buildings that were occupied by the Presidency side, I would only refer to the map and indicate that the line was the confrontation line and the Presidency and Serb side were occupying buildings very close on either side of that confrontation line. I can't tell you specific buildings. The disposition of forces was, from a military viewpoint, interesting in that there were more infantry on both sides than you would expect elsewhere around the perimeter of the city because, clearly, heavy weapons were not useful in that urban environment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, could you tell us, considering that you were in that area, what was -- what were the weapons of the BH army? How were they armed? And what were they wearing? What were the members of the BH army wearing in that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may start with the weapons. The majority of weapons used were small arms, mortars. And the Presidency side also had available anti-aircraft weapons which they used in the direct fire mode. They also had available to them three T-54 tanks, but they were generally located elsewhere in the city. But they were deployed to Nedzarici on a number of occasions. As to clothing, there was a mixture of what I would call "vestiges" of uniform. Many were wearing what I would term as civilian clothes because military uniform was not available to them since they had not been serving in the military when the conflict began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, when you told us that the observation post was removed, was withdrawn, from the area of the Nedzarici, are you saying to us that after withdrawing this observation post, you, as UNMOs, no longer received information about the consequences of operations and activity of the Presidency forces and the BH army in this area? When I say you no longer received reports, you were not informed about the consequences of these operations, of their actions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not quite true because you will recall that I had requested the use of mobile patrols which were able to enter the area from within the city on the Presidency side. The area of Nedzarici was extremely close to the road leading to the airport, and I used this road frequently, as did my UNMOs. And I fully appreciated the sensitivity of this area when talking to General Galic and would listen attentively to any observations that he had over pressures in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, could you confirm to us that in the area where you marked the confrontation line, when we are speaking of Nedzarici, this area has above it -- is dominated by buildings of the Presidency forces, that is buildings in Alipasino Polje and in Vojnicko Polje, and between them is also the Mojmilo hill which was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tenure, did you receive reports that from the area of Mojmilo hill there were snipers active, BH army snipers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of the area of Nedzarici and the front line, could you tell us which army formation was located in the area of Mojmilo, Alipasino Polje and Vojnicko Polje on the side of the Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot tell you the name of the units deployed in that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the positions of the command posts of the unit that was active in that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you confirm to us that in that area, and I am specifically talking about the road that you used, were there police checkpoints there? Was there police there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The checkpoint which had direct effect upon the UN was that checkpoint operated by the Serbs. There was, of course, a front line manned by the Presidency side, but their checkpoint was not as active as that operated by the Serb side. If you are referring to police checkpoints, I would suggest to you that they were military checkpoints operated by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, during your tenure in the Sarajevo area, and we are specifically speaking about this area, were there police forces on both sides on the positions? Did you see them there? Could you perhaps confirm this to us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regarded the front lines of both sides as the confrontation line, and those manning the confrontation line on both sides were military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, could you tell us, what was the depth of the front in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the populated areas, residential areas? Could you perhaps tell us about the dispositions of the troops in a populated area of a unit, of a battalion or a brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the advantage of seeing operational maps belonging to both sides, and in accordance with all military procedure, each side would mark areas of control allocated to individual units. The majority of the maps I saw indicated units of the size of regiment in the British Army, but within this context, they would be brigades. Consequently, one would expect to see, behind the front line, areas of logistic support and command and control. The depth of those activities on the Bosnian side would be variable according to the location of the front line. But to use Nedzarici as an example, the depth would be about 500 to 600 yards. One would expect logistic elements to the rear of that and command and control to the rear of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, would you agree with me, bearing in mind what you said, that the firing positions and disposition of the brigades, the command posts, the logistical support and other military resources, and here we are talking also about the storage ammunition warehouses, these represent legitimate military targets as such?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see those as legitimate military targets, but I would add the caveat that little ammunition would be stored anywhere close to the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, during your tenure in Sarajevo, could you tell us what was the first -- what was the strength of the 1st Corps of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the second part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the second part of the -- yes, it will. It was a request from the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many brigades were included in the 1st Corps of the BH army in Sarajevo in the time -- at the time when you were there, when you were the commander there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact number, but considering the size of the front line and remembering the operational maps that I had the opportunity of viewing, there were a considerable number because there required to be to provide the defence the Presidency side required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, since you agreed with me that the positions of the brigades, the firing positions, command post, logistical support and other military resources, are legitimate military targets, you agreed with me that, as part of the 1st Corps, there were many troops. Could you tell us how many brigades were there and where were they deployed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have answered that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you cannot give us a precise number. If I tell you that there are documents and reports of the UN saying that there were 12 to 14 brigades as part of the 1st Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: My learned colleague has asked the question twice, has got the same answer, that the witness does not remember. And then informing the witness what other documents might say is inappropriate and deserving of such little weight as to be inadmissible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, when you earlier answered that question, would that mean that any further specification is beyond your knowledge or... ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not beyond my knowledge, but I have forgotten how many units were deployed in the 1st Corps in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is not in your memory any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, if it is a matter of memory, I would allow Ms. Pilipovic to refresh the memory of the witness. And at the same time, add to that, Ms. Pilipovic, that the Chamber expects the Defence to finish the cross-examination shortly after the next break. And since I do know that you have split up the cross-examination, I do not know what will be your part or what will be the part of Mr. Piletta-Zanin but I thought it the right time to remind you that it would be somewhere at 1.00, 5 to 10 minutes past 1.00, that the Defence is expected to conclude its cross-examination. If you want further details, after looking into more details, the Prosecution took approximately two hours and three-quarters of an hour, after we deducted time which was not really available to put questions to the witness. I did a similar thing to the Defence, and that would mean that at the end of the next break, you would have used two hours and three-quarters of an hour and that would be the same. So I would grant you an additional 50 minutes because you do not know what kind of interventions, such as the one presently created by the Chamber, would cause as further delay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday we had the information that the examination-in-chief lasted for four hours, but in order not to waste time, we will check that during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I said that in general terms. And then, later on, I said that I would be a bit more precise in deducting whatever should be deducted and that finally comes to a bit less than three hours. And I would grant you a bit over three hours. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, if I may refresh your memory, and if I tell you that there are reports of the United Nations Military Observers, this is a document that is described as a description of the warring factions, this is Exhibit 136P, that the 1st Corps of the BH army had 10 brigades, they had one rear military police, that there was also -- HVO was also part of the 1st Corps and also that within the 1st Corps there were also special forces that were active, that were deployed, that I mean the Ministry of the Interior Special Forces. Is this information acceptable to you, this data?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The question again has many component parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please split it up, unless -- well, the answer is: "That makes sense," which is not quite a clear answer. In general, would you--

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with what was presented then, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mole. During your tenure, were you in a situation to grasp in entirety the disposition or, rather, did you know about the weapons and the armaments that had at their disposal, the 1st Corps of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your memory, of your recollection, could you tell us what heavy weapons did the 1st Corps of the BH army have?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The availability of heavy weapons was very limited, in that the few weapons that we monitored represented the majority of the heavy weapons available to the Presidency side. So the majority of weapons elsewhere were infantry and weapons up to a calibre which would be used within a regular infantry regiment. But I have already indicated that there were the three tanks, anti-aircraft weapons, and mortars which we did not have at weapon collection points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, on the basis of your recollection, and you said that it was an acceptable information regarding the number of the brigades inside the part of the Sarajevo which is under the control of the 1st Corps, could you tell us what strategically important positions had those brigades under their control, in your opinion? Or rather, to be more specific, do you know disposition of the brigades of the 1st Corps at the time when you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew at that time which brigades had which areas of responsibility of the front line, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the area of Dobrinja was under the control of the 5th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it as the 5th Motorised Brigade specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your recollection, could you confirm that in the area of Dobrinja there was such a unit as a brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking on the Presidency side?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mole. So in the area of Dobrinja which was under the control of the Presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the area of Zuc was under the control of the 1st Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't recall the name or number of the unit. But if you are suggesting that part of Zuc was controlled by Presidency forces, the answer would be "yes."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, according to you, the areas of the Mojmilo hill and Zuc, were they important strategic points? And what was the visibility from these positions? How visible was the town area from these two location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mojmilo hill gave tactical advantage overlooking the front line. Zuc gave to those that possessed it control of high ground overlooking the whole city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Mr. Mole, that the area of Mount Igman was also under the BH army control?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, you spoke about an observation post which was set up in the area in the south-eastern part of Sarajevo. Let me remind you, at that time it was Mr. Harding who was the Senior Military Observer, and who also testified before this Tribunal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you be in a position to give me a number for that observation post or are you talking of one which we were attempting to set up in the south-eastern part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about the observation post, yes, that you were attempting to set up.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you were unable to set it up because you had problems with local commanders in the area of Stari Grad, the Old Town, that is the south-eastern part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area where we were attempting to place an observation post was relatively unpopulated, for it was up the hill and away from the city itself. But it fell in the area of responsibility of a brigade in that region, and that brigade felt under significant pressure from the Serb side and were not keen on an observation post being placed there. We never have trouble with the commanders because we don't command them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, did you have any problems with local commanders, that is, the commanders who were not active as part of the BH army but were still operating in the area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people that I dealt with on this particular incident were part of the Presidency forces, as far as I could tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tenure, did you ever receive any information regarding the activity of the paramilitary forces in the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me refresh your memory, Mr. Mole. In your statement, the one that you gave in April on page 0098 -- I am sorry, we didn't get the number of the page. You spoke about Mr. Juka as a criminal.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we must identify what we mean by "paramilitary forces."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that there was a unit whose commander was Juka, who was a criminal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he work within the framework of the BH army or on his own?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that there was considerable conflict between some elements, of which this is one, of the Presidency forces. His exact relationship with the Presidency forces is difficult for an outsider to analyse, but that the Presidency forces had concerns about his activities, I would suggest that is very true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that in this area, the area which was monitored by the Papa OP observers, that there were other such units that were acting on their own?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The degree of their military activity independent of Presidency forces would be extremely difficult to analyse. But I am aware that the command and control of the Presidency side was weak as regards some of its subunits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that in the area of Sarajevo where you attempted to set up an observation post, a brigade was active: The 10th Mountain Brigade was active in that area, the one that was under the command of Caco? Did you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not information specific to the name of the brigade nor the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we spoke about the military formation commanded by Juka, you said that you had information that there were other such units as well. Were you aware of their deployment? Did you know where their command posts were located?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know the location of all command posts for all the military formations within Sarajevo. And a more detailed knowledge was available to me from my subcommander, Flight Lieutenant Harding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "a more detailed knowledge," what exactly do you mean? What kind of more detailed knowledge did you get from subcommander Harding regarding the disposition of these military forces, these military units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Areas of control, disposition, weapons, commanders, he would have more information than me, but it was available to me, should I ask it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, during your tenure, were you aware of the fact that there was a sniper unit within the BH Army Corps there referred to as Seve?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, its name does not remind me of a particular unit, but that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there were snipers on all sides, that was true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get any information from your observers regarding the firing positions of the snipers who were active as part of the BH Army 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had presented to us complaints from both sides relating to sniping, but without sounding trite, I would indicate to you that we prioritised what work we did, and although sniping was an unpleasant experience, we were much more concerned with the use of heavy weapons and the suppression of the use of those weapons. We tended to regard sniping as a hazard of the job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, can you explain to us your view of the sniper activity? You say that it was a hazard of the job. What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sniping was an experience which one dealt with every day in virtually all locations within the city. Obviously, the use of high ground and locations which give good field of view would be used for sniping on both sides. But I say again its priority to us in an area where there was no ceasefire and was constantly under fire from indirect fire weapons, sniping was, in priority terms, quite low.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, you said that one way of reporting was through the use of patrols. Did they provide you with information on sniping incidents as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you verify such information that you received?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refer you back to my answer I have just given, that we were limited in time and resources and we tended to concentrate on the use of heavy weapons. But we did apply ourselves to incidents of sniping on both sides, should we have the resources to do so. But you will appreciate that it is extremely difficult to assess the intended objective of a round that is fired into or out of a front line and then declare that it was sniping. Much of the small arms fire that was experienced in Sarajevo was loosely termed as "sniping," but I challenge anybody to be sure that rounds coming at you are as a result of sniping as opposed to the normal conflict. It's a very fine line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mole. You confirmed the existence of a number of brigades which were part of the 1st BH Army Corps. Can you now tell us how many troops the BH Army Corps consisted of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember with any accuracy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to go back to your interpretation of sniping incidents. Upon receiving an incident report, would you then draft an incident of your own -- I am sorry -- would you then draft a report on your own, once you have received reports from the field, from the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you make the assumption that the general level of activity within the city was peaceful and, therefore, any rounds of any calibre being fired anywhere would result in some investigation by either UN military observers or by UNPROFOR police. Nothing could be further from the truth. To understand that, you have to comprehend that -- excuse me. You have to comprehend that -- excuse me. The activity level was intense and only varied in level. It never ceased to the situation where we could respond to every incident, as you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Mole. During your mandate, did you make any attempts to establish the number of legitimate military targets in the town of Sarajevo which was under the BH army control?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was no more my job to do that than it was to do the same on the Serb side. I have already identified what my raison d'etre was within the city, and it did not include what you would term as "military information."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that it was not, strictly speaking, within your competence, does that mean that you did not have accurate information on the number of legitimate military targets in that part of the city and their location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it was outside my competence. I am drawing a distinct line between what is intelligence, and that is definitely something that the UN was not there to collect, as opposed to other information which, by I having it, permitted us to achieve our objectives which I have already identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, during the examination-in-chief by my learned colleague yesterday, you were shown Exhibit 618, your monthly report for the month of December, the one that you did not sign because you didn't stay until the end of the month. In this report you speak about the shelling, that is, you confirm what was established in the monthly report. Specifically, I am referring to the 7th and the 8th of December, also the 9th and 10th of December, the 11th and the 12th. You say that the shells were falling all over the city, and you confirmed that information as being accurate. Is it so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, can you now confirm that that period of time coincided with the fighting for Otes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The beginning of the month of December, did it also see the fighting for the Mount Zuc?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the area of Trebevic and Hresa, was there any fighting going on there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main area or concentration of fire was definitely within the Otes area but I would not dismiss fighting elsewhere on the perimeter of the city, as indeed I have agreed there was fighting in Zuc area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, in your statement on page 00908156, you declared that there was a policy which was intended to prevent the enemy from taking up more territory, the policy which was being implemented by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Can you explain to us what exactly is it that you meant by this phrase?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I appreciate my learned colleague giving page numbers. Unfortunately, they are of the B/C/S version. Perhaps she might indicate firstly which statement and whether it is approximately halfway through the statement or a quarter of the way through. I would be grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the statement of the 1st, the 2nd and the 3rd of September, 1997. The page is in B/C/S, but perhaps we can have the break now and that will allow me to locate the portion of the text in the English original and, hence, be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would, at least, be avoiding time spent on locating. Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you seem not to agree that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I fully agree with that, however, I do not agree with your calculation on the hours spent in examination. I think we are closer to four hours than three hours. I don't know whether you have taken into account two previous days in respect of which the total would be two and-a-half hours. I am talking about the days of the 3rd and the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I would not forget Mr. Mole being here on the 3rd and the 7th of June. Could you please indicate to me how many minutes you locate on each of these days? The 3rd of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards to the 3rd of June, I think it was from 1420 until 1530. For the 7th of June, from 9.00 until 11.30. We have deducted the necessary breaks each time. That is according to my calculations. As of today, I also made some calculations compared to yesterday. There were 42 pages of intervention by Mr. Ierace, which brings us to another two hours if we calculate two minutes per page. It means that we have 84 minutes left and that brings us to four and-a-half hours. The pages in questions are 2.069 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You switched yesterday from today. Yesterday, how many minutes did you calculate of the 2nd of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took into account yesterday. Yesterday, I calculated 42 pages. If we calculate three minutes -- I don't have the time indicator on my screen any more. That would be two hours. If we calculate then two minutes per page, then it would be the total of one and-a-half hours. I am talking about 2.068 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry, the interpreters cannot follow the numbers at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is clear to me you are referring to page numbers. And today you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. Mr. Ierace did not take the flow. I am not going to charge him with anything that happened today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what time did you deduct on the 3rd of June for interventions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the breaks or the interventions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Interventions which prevented the other party -- longer interventions which prevented the other party from asking questions and getting answers to those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None, strictly speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will go through my calculations again during the break. I think that I would finally not agree with your calculations, but please keep in mind that there is not much time left, and I will go over the calculations again. We will adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Ms. Pilipovic, I should indicate to the parties that my refreshment course in mathematics showed that - I improved during the break - you have -- if you could finish today, it would be fine, but you would be entitled to a couple of minutes more tomorrow morning. But as I indicated before, it is not always necessary to use all the time, but you would have approximately, let's say, a little bit over one hour left. So I apologise for informing you wrongly before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For my learned colleague, before the break, I asked Mr. Mole to comment on his statement from the 1st of September, and the page was 00520512. That was the first paragraph, last line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, you used a sentence saying that there was a policy of containment and that it was implemented by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Could you please explain this? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it as a military expression, in that I perceived that there was neither the will nor the intention for the Serbs to alter the position of the front lines significantly because to do so would jeopardise their military position, whereas to do nothing and retain the status quo achieved their objective sufficiently. Hence I use the term "policy of containment" to explain that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mole. When you said that in December there were battles fought for Mount Zuc, could you tell us from which parts of town of the city there was -- there were troops maneuvering in the direction of Mount Zuc?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you refer to the requirement for reinforcement on Zuc from the Presidency side?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mole.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that obviously occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this reinforcement in the direction of Mount Zuc, and bearing in mind the disposition of the brigades of the 1st Corps of the BH army could have been from the directions of Buljakov Potok, Buca Potok, that is, from the populated areas of the city?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, in your statement you spoke of the interest of the Presidency to restrict people or citizens, population, entering and leaving the city. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't always within the gift of the Presidency to make those decisions because it required both sides to agree for movements in and out of the city. But I believe that the Presidency tended towards retention of their population within the confines of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please clarify what were the reasons for this, as you say it, that the Presidency had this interest to keep the population inside the confines of the city?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any leeching of the population would weaken the numbers available to the Presidency as fighting individuals, and when it related to noncombatants, there was, I believe, a tendency to require them to stay within the city because the status quo, which I have already explained to you, suited the Presidency's position apropos the strategic relevance of Sarajevo within the context of all solutions within Bosnia. The Presidency benefited from the city being deemed to be under siege for sympathy from outside Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
